lead: Bayes theorem tells how to update a belief (prior probability) when new evidence arrives. It gives a posterior probability that combines the prior with the likelihood of the evidence. In classification we use the posterior to pick the most probable class (MAP) or we estimate model parameters that make the observed data most likely (MLE). These ideas appear in spam filters, medical diagnosis, and any system that must learn from data while handling uncertainty.
prereq: You need: basic probability from Unit 1. Decision tree learning concepts are useful for understanding information gain, but not required here.

blocks.text: Bayes theorem relates four probabilities: the prior P(C), the likelihood P(X|C), the evidence P(X), and the posterior P(C|X). It is written as P(C|X)=P(X|C)·P(C)÷P(X). Here C is a class label and X is a feature vector. The theorem shows how to revise the prior belief about a class after observing X.

blocks.where: P(C|X) is the posterior probability of class C given data X; P(X|C) is the likelihood of observing X if class C is true; P(C) is the prior probability of class C; P(X) is the marginal probability of X over all classes.

blocks.text: When we compare two classes, P(X) is the same for both and cancels out. Therefore we can rank classes by the product P(X|C)·P(C) without computing P(X). This cancellation is the key to fast MAP classification.

items: Prior P(C) reflects knowledge before seeing the data.
Likelihood P(X|C) measures how well the data fits the class.
Posterior P(C|X) combines both to give updated belief.

blocks.text: Bayes theorem is the foundation of many classifiers, such as the Naive Bayes model (chapter 3.3) and Bayesian belief networks (chapter 3.5).

MAP chooses the class with the highest posterior probability. Formally, we select Ĉ = arg max_C P(C|X). Using Bayes theorem and cancelling P(X), this becomes Ĉ = arg max_C P(X|C)·P(C). The term P(C) is called the prior; if all classes are equally likely, MAP reduces to the maximum likelihood rule.

items: Compute the prior P(C) for each class (may come from training frequencies).
Compute the likelihood P(X|C) for the observed X.
Multiply prior and likelihood for each class.
Pick the class with the largest product.

blocks.text: A common exam mistake is to forget that P(X) cancels when comparing classes, leading to an extra denominator that changes the ranking.

blocks.where: Ĉ is the predicted class; P(X|C) is the class‑conditional likelihood; P(C) is the prior probability of class C.

blocks.text: MLE finds the parameter values θ that make the observed data most probable. For a data set X={x₁,…,x_n} the likelihood is L(θ)=∏_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i|θ). The MLE θ̂ maximises L(θ) or, equivalently, the log‑likelihood ℓ(θ)=∑ log P(x_i|θ).

items: Take the natural log to obtain ℓ(θ)=∑ log P(x_i|θ).
Differentiate ℓ(θ) with respect to θ and set the derivative to zero.

blocks.text: For a Bernoulli coin with unknown bias θ, the likelihood after observing h heads and t tails is θ^{h}(1-θ)^{t}. Differentiating the log‑likelihood gives θ̂ = h/(h+t). This is the familiar frequency estimate.

items: MLE does not use a prior; it only depends on the observed data.
If a prior is added, the resulting estimate is called MAP.
MLE can be biased for small samples; MAP often reduces bias.

figure.caption: Block diagram showing how prior and likelihood are multiplied to obtain the posterior; the denominator P(X) is omitted when ranking classes.

examples.question: A biased coin is tossed 10 times and shows 7 heads. (a) Find the maximum likelihood estimate of the coin's bias θ. (b) Assuming a Beta(2,2) prior for θ (Laplace smoothing), compute the MAP estimate.
steps: MLE: θ̂_MLE = number of heads ÷ total tosses = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7.
Beta(2,2) prior (Laplace smoothing) adds one pseudo‑count to each outcome.
examples.answer: MLE of the bias is 0.7; MAP estimate with a Beta(2,2) prior (Laplace smoothing) is 0.667.
examples.check:
h=7
n=10
mle=h/n
map=(h+1)/(n+2)
print(mle)
print(map)

traps: Treating P(X) as a constant but forgetting to cancel it when comparing class posteriors leads to wrong MAP rankings.
Confusing the uniform prior (Beta(1,1)) with Laplace smoothing; the former gives MAP = MLE, while Laplace adds one pseudo‑count to each outcome.

Using the number of heads divided by total tosses for MAP without adding the prior pseudo‑counts, which yields the same value as MLE and may be marked incorrect if the question expects Laplace smoothing.
Neglecting to convert percentages to fractions before plugging into formulas, causing unit errors.

quiz.q: State Bayes theorem in terms of prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior.
Explain why the evidence term P(X) can be ignored when selecting the most probable class.
quiz.a: P(X) is the same for all classes, so it does not affect the relative ordering; the arg‑max depends only on the product P(X|C)·P(C).

quiz.q: A dataset has 30 spam emails and 70 ham emails. A new email contains the word “discount”. The likelihood P("discount"|spam)=0.4 and P("discount"|ham)=0.1. Compute the MAP class assuming the priors are given by the dataset frequencies.
quiz.a: Prior spam=30/100=0.3, prior ham=0.7. Compute products: spam:0.4×0.3=0.12; ham:0.1×0.7=0.07. MAP chooses spam.

quiz.q: For a Bernoulli process with 4 heads and 6 tails, find the MLE of the success probability.
Compare the effect of a strong prior favouring class A on MAP classification versus MLE classification in a scenario where the data weakly supports class B.
quiz.a: A strong prior increases P(A), so MAP may still select A even if the likelihood for B is higher; MLE ignores priors and will select B because it maximises the likelihood alone.

quiz.q: If two classes have identical likelihoods for an observation, how does MAP decide between them?
quiz.a: MAP chooses the class with the higher prior probability.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Bayesian updating underlies online recommendation engines and fraud detection where models must adapt to streaming data. Research extends MAP and MLE to deep generative models and variational inference. Recent curricula link these ideas to probabilistic programming languages such as PyMC or Stan. To go further, explore Bayesian neural networks and the Expectation‑Maximisation algorithm for latent variable models.
